title: Job Scheduling — dynamic resource allocation and graceful decommissioning (Apache Spark documentation)

claims.text: During a shuffle a Spark executor writes its map output to local disk and then acts as the server for those files when other executors fetch them, which is the structural reason an executor cannot be released simply because it has no running tasks.

Apache Spark's own documentation names the failure directly: if dynamic allocation removes an executor before a shuffle is fully consumed — the straggler case — the shuffle files that executor wrote must be recomputed unnecessarily.

spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled is false by default in open-source Spark; dynamic allocation adds and removes executors in response to load rather than holding a fixed cluster for the life of the application.

Spark offers three ways to stop an executor's shuffle output dying with it: an external shuffle service that serves shuffle files beyond the executor's lifetime, shuffle tracking (spark.dynamicAllocation.shuffleTracking.enabled) which keeps executors holding needed shuffle data alive, and graceful decommissioning which migrates blocks before exit.

Graceful decommissioning — spark.decommission.enabled together with spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled, both false by default — preserves an executor's state by migrating its shuffle blocks to a peer (or to configured fallback storage) before the executor actually exits.

Spark exposes a pluggable shuffle storage interface via spark.shuffle.sort.io.plugin.class, which is the documented extension point through which a platform can redirect shuffle data to reliable remote storage instead of executor-local disk.

Executors holding cached data are not removed by dynamic allocation by default, which is a separate scale-down blocker from shuffle data and is governed by spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout.
